tools.name: Pacer
tools.subtitle: min per mark
tools.help:
Pacer
Times a practice paper against a plan.

1. Enter minutes, marks and the
   checkpoint size.
2. EXE starts the clock.
3. F1 logs a mark, F2 pauses.

The gap line says how far ahead or
behind the plan you are.

Keys: EXE start/stop, F1 mark, F2
pause, F3 finish, EXIT back.
tools.summary: Minutes per mark, checkpoint times, and a live gap line: “Behind by 1m20s”.
tools.body: Enter the length of the paper and how many marks it carries. Bench splits it into checkpoints and then runs the clock against them, four redraws a second so the battery is not asked for more.
points: Setup: total minutes, total marks, marks per checkpoint.
90 minutes and 80 marks gives 1.125 min/mark and eight checkpoints.
Run: F1 logs a mark, F2 pauses, F3 finishes. The gap line is the point.
Done: total time and the final gap, nothing to write down.
tools.leadCaption: Finished: total time and final gap
shots: The plan: min/mark and every checkpoint time
Running: clock, marks logged, gap line
Finished: total time and final gap

tools.name: Cards
tools.subtitle: flashcards
tools.help:
Cards
Flashcards with a Leitner schedule.

A deck is one file in Bench/cards,
one card per line:
   question | answer

Right answers move a card to the
next box, wrong ones send it back.
Progress is saved when the session
ends, never during it.

Keys: EXE reveal/mark, F1 right,
F2 wrong, EXIT back.
tools.summary: A flashcard drill over a plain text deck, spaced across three boxes.
tools.body: Decks are text you can write anywhere: one card a line, question and answer split by a vertical bar. Right moves a card up a box, wrong sends it back to box 1, and boxes 2 and 3 come round less often.
points: “What is the unit of impulse? | N s” is a whole card.
500 cards a deck, 120 characters a side; a broken line is reported with its number.
Progress is keyed by a hash of the question, so editing an answer keeps its box.
Saved once, when the session ends, never inside the loop.
tools.leadCaption: The answer, and F1 / F2 to grade it
shots: A deck: cards per box and when it is due
The answer, and F1 / F2 to grade it

tools.name: Notes
tools.subtitle: Markdown
tools.help:
Notes
Reads .md and .txt from Bench/notes.

Markdown headings, lists, quotes,
bold and code are drawn in the
palette. Long lines wrap; the wrap
width is a setting.

Keys: UP/DOWN scroll, EXE page down,
ALPHA search, F2 headings, EXIT.
tools.summary: Read text and a Markdown subset from the calculator's storage, with search.
tools.body: Drop .md and .txt files into Bench/notes and read them on the calculator. Headings, bold, italic, code, lists, quotes and checkboxes are styled with colour and rules rather than extra fonts, so nothing has to be installed.
points: Up to 32 KiB a file, long lines wrapped to the screen or to a set width.
F1 search, F2 next hit, F3 the heading list, F4 back to the top.
Characters the calculator font lacks are drawn as ? and counted in the footer.
tools/md2bench.py maps typographic symbols down to ASCII before you copy.
tools.leadCaption: A Markdown note: headings, bold, a list
shots: A Markdown note: headings, bold, a list
Jump to any heading with F3
Scrolling a long note by page

tools.name: Study log
tools.subtitle: minutes per day
tools.help:
Study log
What you did, for how long, and
on which day, in a text file you
can also edit by hand:

  2026-10-31 25 pacer

A broken line is skipped and
counted, never added up wrongly.

F1 adds a session: type the
minutes, UP/DOWN picks the tool,
LEFT/RIGHT moves between the three
fields, EXE saves it. F2 deletes
the last one, which is the mistake
you will make.

Bench cannot read the calendar, so
a new entry takes the day after the
newest one in the log; UP/DOWN on
the day moves it. The file is
written once, when you leave.
tools.summary: A plain text log of what you studied and for how long, with totals, days logged and the longest streak.
tools.body: One line a session, in a file you can also write by hand. The screen adds up the minutes, counts the days and finds the longest run of consecutive days; a line it cannot read is skipped and counted rather than silently binned.
points: “2026-10-31 25 pacer” is a whole entry.
F1 adds one: minutes, then UP/DOWN for the tool, EXE to save.
The file is written once, when you leave the screen.
Bench cannot read the calendar, so an entry takes the day after the newest.
tools.leadCaption: Two sessions, with the totals above them
shots: Two sessions, with the totals above them
Adding a session: minutes, tool, day
The empty state says where the file lives

tools.name: Pi game
tools.subtitle: digits from memory
tools.help:
Pi game
The digits of pi, from memory.

The digits you have earned stay on
screen, grouped five at a time. Type
the next ones and press EXE: every
digit right moves you along, and the
first wrong one costs a life.

Three lives. F2 shows the next digit
and costs one, so a hint is never
free. When the lives are gone the
page shows how far you got and the
best of this session.

Nothing is written to the card: the
best score is gone when the add-in
closes.

Keys: digits, DEL, EXE check, F1
again, F2 hint, EXIT back.
tools.summary: The digits of pi, from memory, five at a time and three lives deep.
tools.body: The digits you have already earned stay on screen, grouped in fives, and you type the next run and press EXE. Every digit right moves you on; the first wrong one costs a life. F2 gives the next digit away and costs a life too, so a hint is never free.
points: Three lives, and the score is how many digits you reached.
Nothing is written to the card: the best of the session goes when the add-in closes.
A wrong digit is shown against the right one, so the mistake is the lesson.
Keys: digits, DEL, EXE to check, F1 to start again, F2 for a hint.
tools.leadCaption: Three digits in, two lives left
shots: Three digits in, two lives left
A wrong digit, shown against the right one
Out of lives: the digits reached

tools.name: Formula book
tools.subtitle: IB booklets
tools.help:
Formula book
The IB formula and data booklets,
as plain text on the card.

Copy them into Bench/formulas, one
.txt per booklet. The list shows
every file in that folder, so a
booklet you write yourself appears
there too.

In the book: UP/DOWN scroll a line,
LEFT/RIGHT jump a section, F1 goes
to the top. Headings are red, blue
and ink by level.

# is a booklet title, ## a topic,
### a sub-topic, one space after
the hashes.

Keys: EXE open, LEFT/RIGHT section,
F1 top, EXIT back.
tools.summary: The IB formula and data booklets as plain text on the calculator, one file per booklet.
tools.body: Copy the booklets into Bench/formulas, one .txt per booklet, and the list shows every file in that folder, including one you write yourself. Inside a booklet, UP and DOWN scroll a line, LEFT and RIGHT jump a section, and F1 goes back to the top.
points: # is a booklet title, ## a topic, ### a sub-topic, one space after the hashes.
Headings are red, blue and ink by level, so a topic is findable at a glance.
AA HL, Physics 2025 and Chemistry 2025 are in docs/samples/formulas to copy across.
Those three are typed by hand and marked as needing a human proofread before use.
tools.leadCaption: A topic heading, then the formulas under it
shots: A topic heading, then the formulas under it
RIGHT jumps to the next topic

tools.name: Function
tools.subtitle: x and f(x)
tools.help:
Function table
A table and a value for f(x).

1. Pick a slot f, g, h, p, q, r.
2. EXE types the expression on the
   keyboard: x, pi, e, + - * / ^,
   sin cos tan ln log sqrt abs.
3. F1 opens the table.

In the table: LEFT/RIGHT move the
start, F1 changes the step, F2 the
row count, EXE probes one value.
F4 switches degrees and radians;
the mode shows in the title bar.

Slots are written to
Bench/state/exprs.txt when you
leave the tool.

Keys: EXE edit, F1 table, F3 clear.
tools.summary: One engine for x, pi, e and twenty functions, behind a table and a probe.
tools.body: Type an expression once on the on-screen keyboard and keep it in one of six slots: f, g, h, p, q, r. A shunting-yard parser holds its operator stack in a fixed 32 entries, so a long expression cannot overflow the calculator's stack, and an error names the column it failed at.
points: Implicit multiplication: 3x, 2(x+1), (x+1)(x-1), 2pi.
A table of x and f(x) from a start value, a step and a count; F2 probes one value.
Six expressions live in RAM and reach Bench/state/exprs.txt when you leave the tool.
tools.leadCaption: Six expressions, and a table of one of them
shots: The six slots and their expressions
A table of x against f(x)

tools.name: Triangle
tools.subtitle: sides, angles
tools.help:
Triangle
Three sides and three angles. Fill
in what you know and leave the rest
blank.

Give any three values, at least one
a side: SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS all
solve, and the fields fill in.

SSA - two sides and an angle not
between them - can have two answers.
The title bar then says so and F2
swaps between the two triangles.

Area and perimeter are under the
fields.  F3 degrees, F4 radians.

Keys: arrows move, digits type,
EXE solves, F1 clears.
tools.summary: Any three of the six values in, every side, angle, the area and the perimeter out.
tools.body: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and SSA go through the law of cosines and the law of sines. The SSA case says when there are two triangles instead of quietly picking one, and the six boxes sit in the shape of the triangle: a b c over A B C, each angle under the side it is opposite.
points: 3, 4, 5 gives C = 90°, A = 36.87°, area 6 and perimeter 12.
SSA with a = 10, b = 15, A = 30° reports two triangles; F2 swaps between them.
Worked lines for the cosine rule and the sine rule.
F3 degrees, F4 radians, and the unit is in the title bar.
tools.leadCaption: 3, 4, 5: the right angle, the area, the perimeter
shots: 3, 4, 5: the right angle, the area, the perimeter
The SSA case, with both triangles available

tools.name: Polynomials
tools.subtitle: roots, expand
tools.help:
Polynomials
Quadratics, expansion and rational
roots.

Three screens, F4 or F2 next and F3
back:
  Quadratic  a, b, c give the
             discriminant, both roots
             and the vertex.
  Expand     (ax + b)^n to degree 8.
  Roots      c0..cn as coefficients;
             whole and half roots are
             found, the rest is shown.

Arrows move between fields, digits
type, DEL deletes, F1 clears.  F2 on
the roots screen adds a coefficient.

Rounding is half up on the digits.
tools.summary: Quadratics, expansion and division, with the discriminant, the vertex and the factors.
tools.body: Three screens over one fixed-size polynomial type: a quadratic that shows the discriminant, both roots, the vertex and the factor pair; an expansion of (ax + b)^n term by term; and a coefficient list whose rational roots are hunted by the rational root theorem.
points: x² - 5x + 6: discriminant 1, roots 3 and 2, vertex (2.5, -0.25).
x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 factors as (x - 3)(x - 2)(x - 1).
Divide x³ - 2x² - 4 by x - 3: quotient x² + x + 3, remainder 5.
Coefficients are typed rather than parsed, because the keypad has no letters for x².
tools.leadCaption: A quadratic: discriminant, roots, vertex, factor pair
shots: A quadratic: discriminant, roots, vertex, factor pair

tools.name: Root finder
tools.subtitle: bisect, Newton
tools.help:
Root finder
Solves f(x) = 0 one step at a time,
so the convergence is visible.

F2 picks the method:
  bisection needs a and b with a
    sign change between them
  Newton needs one guess x0
  secant needs two guesses x0, x1

F3 solves. The table lists n, x and
f(x); the plot marks every iterate.

Radians always, whatever the angle
setting says. Tolerance 1e-6, at most
50 steps.

F4 lists the last eight answers, so a
root does not vanish when the fields
change. Nothing is written to storage.

Keys: EXE edits f or solves, F1 clears,
F2 method, F4 history, arrows move
and scroll.
tools.summary: f(x) = 0 one step at a time, with every iterate in a table and marked on the curve.
tools.body: Bisection, Newton and the secant method over an expression from the expression engine. Newton takes its slope from a central difference with a step of 1e-6, so no derivative has to be typed, and the table of n, x, f(x) and the step size shows the error falling rather than asserting that it does.
points: Newton on x² - 2 from 1: 1.5, 1.416667, 1.414216, root 1.414214 in four steps.
Bisection on [1, 2] reaches the same root in twenty.
No sign change and a zero slope are refused with a sentence, not guessed at.
Radians always, said in the title bar, with a 50-step cap.
tools.leadCaption: Newton: four iterates and the plot that marks them
shots: Newton: four iterates and the plot that marks them
A bracket with no sign change

tools.name: Sequences
tools.subtitle: terms, sums
tools.help:
Sequences
Arithmetic and geometric terms,
their sums, and binomials.

Three screens, F4 next and F3 back.

  Arithmetic  a, d, n: the nth term
              and the sum, then the
              first few terms.
  Geometric   a, r, n: as above, plus
              the sum to infinity when
              |r| < 1.
  Binomial    n choose k exactly, and
              row n of Pascal.

Terms count from 1, so the first term
is n = 1.  C(n,k) is refused rather
than rounded when it passes 64 bits.

Keys: arrows move, digits type,
EXE solves, F1 clears.
tools.summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, the sum to infinity, and binomial coefficients.
tools.body: Terms and partial sums for both kinds of sequence, with the first few terms listed under the answer so the pattern is visible. The binomial screen works through Pascal's row, one term of (ax + b)^n, and a coefficient at a chosen power.
points: u₁ = 3, d = 4: u₁₀ = 39 and S₁₀ = 210.
u₁ = 2, r = 3: u₅ = 162 and S₅ = 242; with r = 0.5 the sum to infinity of 8 is 16.
C(n,k) cancels before it multiplies, so C(62,31) still fits in 64 bits.
A coefficient that would pass 64 bits is refused rather than printed wrong.
tools.leadCaption: Arithmetic: u₁₀ and S₁₀, with the terms underneath
shots: Arithmetic: u₁₀ and S₁₀, with the terms underneath
Pascal's row and a binomial coefficient

tools.name: Complex
tools.subtitle: a + bi
tools.help:
Complex numbers
Two numbers a and b, one operation
at a time.

F2 picks the operation: a + b,
a - b, a x b, a / b and a ^ n, where
n is the real part of b.

The result is written three ways:
rectangular (-1 + 2i), its modulus
and argument, and polar form.

F3 shows the argument in degrees,
F4 in radians.

Keys: arrows move, digits type,
DEL deletes, F1 clears, EXIT home.
tools.summary: Rectangular, modulus-and-argument and polar form on one screen.
tools.body: Two numbers, one operation at a time, and the answer written three ways so it is obvious they are the same number. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and integer powers, with the argument taken in the angle mode you picked.
points: 1 + i has modulus 1.414214 and argument 45°; (1 + i)⁴ = -4.
Dividing by 0 + 0i says “not a number” instead of printing an infinity.
F2 cycles the operation, F3 and F4 pick degrees or radians.
tools.leadCaption: A product in all three forms
shots: A product in all three forms

tools.name: Number theory
tools.subtitle: gcd to CRT
tools.help:
Number theory
Nine functions, each with working.

gcd, lcm, prime test, factorise,
modular inverse, CRT, divisors,
totient and base conversion.

Factorisation shows a progress bar;
EXIT cancels it.

Keys: UP/DOWN choose, EXE open,
EXIT back.
tools.summary: gcd to CRT, in 64-bit integer arithmetic: no floats, no rounding surprises.
tools.body: Nine functions behind one menu, with the working shown where the working is the point, such as Euclid's steps for gcd or an extended gcd. Inputs up to 18 digits are exact.
points: gcd, lcm, extended gcd with Bézout coefficients, modular inverse.
modpow by square and multiply with mulmod, so 2^64 mod 1000 is exact.
Deterministic Miller-Rabin primality test for the whole 64-bit range.
Factor by trial division then Pollard rho, with a progress bar and EXIT to cancel.
Euler's totient and the Chinese remainder theorem, one pair or a whole list.
tools.leadCaption: gcd(84, 36) = 12, Euclid's steps underneath

tools.name: Prime factors
tools.subtitle: factorise n
tools.help:
Prime factors
Type a whole number and press EXE.
The page shows the factorisation
with powers, then the four things
that follow from it.

360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5
  divisors 24, their sum 1170
  totient 96
  square-free part 30

Square-free part is the primes
multiplied with their powers thrown
away: 30 for 360. If it equals the
number, the number is square free.

Up to 18 digits. F2 halves the
number and factors again.

Keys: digits, DEL, F1 clear, F2
halve, EXE factor, EXIT back.
tools.summary: A whole number into prime powers, with the divisors, their sum, the totient and the square-free part.
tools.body: Type a number and press EXE. The page writes the factorisation with powers and then the four things that follow from it, because those are what the questions ask for next: how many divisors there are, what they add up to, the totient, and the square-free part.
points: 360 gives 2³ × 3² × 5, 24 divisors, a divisor sum of 1170, totient 96, square-free part 30.
The square-free part throws the powers away, so it equals the number only when the number is already square free.
Up to 18 digits, worked in integers: no rounding anywhere.
F2 halves the number and factors it again.
tools.leadCaption: 360 as prime powers, then the four numbers that follow
shots: 360 as prime powers, then the four numbers that follow
A number with a high power in it

tools.name: Statistics
tools.subtitle: mean to regression
tools.help:
Statistics
Type a value, press EXE to add it,
and the summary is worked out as
you go. Up to 200 values.

F2 switches between one list and
paired data (x, then y). Pairs give
the line y = a + bx, r and r squared.

F3 picks the quartile method:
  median  halves split through the
          median
  sheet   (n-1)p + 1, interpolated

F4 shows the working for the standard
deviation. F1 clears the list.

Keys: digits type, EXE adds, DEL takes
back a digit or a value.
tools.summary: Type the numbers, read n, mean, median, mode, both quartile methods, the outlier fences and a box plot.
tools.body: The summary updates as you type, which makes a typo visible before you trust the answer. Paired data gives the least squares line, r and r squared; F4 writes the standard deviation out step by step, the way it is marked.
points: 2 4 4 4 5 5 7 9: mean 5, median 4.5, sd 2.000 pop / 2.138 sample.
Quartiles by halves (4 and 6) or by the spreadsheet rule (5.5), one key apart.
Fences at 1 and 9: nothing outside them here, and the count says so.
tools.leadCaption: Eight values, summarised, with a box plot
shots: Eight values, summarised, with a box plot
Pairs: the least squares line, r and r squared
The working behind the standard deviation

tools.name: Base and bits
tools.subtitle: hex, shifts
tools.help:
Bases and bits
One number in base 2 to 36, and
the same number as two's complement
at 8, 16 and 32 bits.

F1 switches between converting
and the bitwise operators.

F3 changes the entry base, or the
operator: AND, OR, XOR, shift left
and shift right. A shift uses the
count in b and refuses 63 or more.

F2 opens the letter keyboard for
digits above 9, since the keypad
has no A to F keys this add-in may
count on. Digits can still be
typed straight in.

Keys: digits type, DEL takes one
back, F4 swaps a and b.
tools.summary: One number in five bases and as two's complement at 8, 16 and 32 bits, plus the bitwise operators.
tools.body: The converting tab shows a value in decimal, hex, octal, binary and base 36 at once, then the same value as a two's complement pattern at the three widths a paper uses. The operator tab puts two numbers side by side in binary and shows the result in decimal and hex, with the bits set.
points: -1 at 8 bits is 1111 1111, and at 32 bits eight F's.
A shift of 63 or more is refused rather than undefined.
tools.leadCaption: 255 in five bases and at three widths
shots: 255 in five bases and at three widths

tools.name: Percentages
tools.subtitle: change, growth
tools.help:
Percentages
Four questions, chosen with UP/DOWN.

Change: from 40 to 46 is a rise
of 15%.

Add or take: 40 with 15% added is
46, and the page shows the working.

Reverse: something costs 34 after
15% off, so it was 40. Dividing by
0.85, not taking 15% back off.

Compound: 500 at 4.5% for 7 years
is 680.43, with interest added each
year. A negative rate depreciates.

A percentage change from zero, and
a 100% discount, have no answer and
the page says why.

Keys: UP/DOWN question, LEFT/RIGHT
field, EXE work out, F1 clear.
tools.summary: Percentage change, add and take, the reverse question, and compound growth, each with its working.
tools.body: Four questions chosen with UP and DOWN, and the page shows the working rather than only the answer. The reverse question divides by what is left after the change instead of taking the percentage back off, which is the mistake it exists to stop.
points: Change: 40 to 46 is a rise of 15%.
Add or take: 40 with 15% added is 46, with the sum written out.
Reverse: something costs 34 after 15% off, so it was 40, not 39.10.
Compound: 500 at 4.5% for 7 years is 680.43; a negative rate depreciates.
A change from zero and a 100% discount have no answer, and the page says which and why.
tools.leadCaption: From 40 to 46: a rise of 15%, with the difference shown
shots: From 40 to 46: a rise of 15%, with the difference shown
The reverse question: 34 after 15% off was 40

tools.name: Uncertainty
tools.subtitle: value and error
tools.help:
Uncertainty
Arithmetic with errors, to 1 or 2
significant figures.

Type a value and its absolute error,
pick an operation, type the second
value and error.

Chain mode keeps the result as the
first value of the next step.

Keys: F1..F3 operation, EXE apply,
EXIT back.
tools.summary: Add, subtract, multiply, divide and raise measured values, errors included.
tools.body: Two values with their errors, one operation, and a result in the shape a physics teacher wants: value, absolute uncertainty, percentage. F1 feeds the result back in as A and you keep going.
points: A + B and A - B add the absolute errors; A * B and A / B add the relative ones.
A ^ n and k * A are covered too, with the exact rule for each.
Rounding is half-up on decimal digits, never on the binary float: 0.15 goes to 0.2.
One figure for the uncertainty, or two when its first digit is 1.
shots: Choosing the operation and the second operand

tools.name: Sig figs
tools.subtitle: round, standard
tools.help:
Sig figs
How many figures, and how to write
them.

UP/DOWN picks a mode, LEFT/RIGHT
changes n, EXE types the number.

Count: leading zeros never count,
and trailing zeros count only after
a decimal point. 0.004560 has 4.

Round: half up on the decimal
digits, so 1234.5 to 3 figures is
1230 = 1.23 x 10^3.

Practice asks a question; type the
count and EXE marks it, F2 moves
on.

Keys: EXE type, F1 clear.
tools.summary: Significant figures counted on the text rather than the value, plus standard form and SI prefixes.
tools.body: Six modes: count the figures, round to a number of figures, round to a number of decimals, standard form, SI prefix, and a practice mode that asks and marks. Figures are counted on the characters you typed, which is why 1200 has two and 1200. has four.
points: 0.004560 has 4 figures and is 4.560 × 10⁻³.
1234.5 to 3 figures is 1230, written 1.23 × 10³.
4560 with a prefix is 4.56 k; 1e-9 is 1.00 n.
Rounding is half-up on the decimal digits, never on the binary float.
tools.leadCaption: Count the figures, then round a third
shots: Counting the figures in a typed number
Count the figures, then round a third

tools.name: SUVAT
tools.subtitle: motion, projectiles
tools.help:
SUVAT and projectiles
Type any three of s, u, v, a and t.
The other two are worked out, with
the equation that gave each one.

Use the arrows to pick a quantity,
type the number, press EXE. DEL on
an empty field un-knows it.

F2 draws the flight path: range,
greatest height and time in the air
for a launch speed, angle and height.

F3 switches g between 9.81 and 10.
Where a quadratic gives two times,
the first is shown and the second
is mentioned under it.

Keys: digits type, EXE keeps, DEL
takes back, F1 starts again.
tools.summary: Give any three of s, u, v, a and t, and the other two appear with the equation that produced them.
tools.body: A constant-acceleration solver that shows its working rather than just the answer: every derived value is marked with a dot, and the equations are listed under the grid. The projectile screen draws the path for a launch speed, angle and height, with the range, the peak and the time in the air.
points: s = 45, u = 0, a = 10: v = 30 m/s and t = 3 s, from v = u + at.
s = 75, u = 20, a = -2: v = 10 m/s, and t = 5 s rather than 15 s.
Where a quadratic gives two times, the second is named under the answer.
20 m/s at 30 degrees from the ground: 35.3 m in 2.04 s.
tools.leadCaption: The flight path for 20 m/s at 30 degrees
shots: Three values in, two out, with the equations
Typed by hand, with the two-time case flagged
The flight path for 20 m/s at 30 degrees

tools.name: Moles
tools.subtitle: mass, gas, conc
tools.help:
Moles and solutions
Five calculations, one per mode:
moles from a mass, concentration,
the gas equation, dilution, and
yield or atom economy.

Each mode opens on a worked
example; F1 puts it back.

The unit under each number is the
one the formula wants: volumes in
dm3, so 25 cm3 is 0.025, and
temperature in kelvin.

R is 8.314, for p in kPa and V in
dm3. A zero where a formula divides
says so instead of printing an
infinity.

Keys: UP/DOWN pick a field, digits
type, F3/F4 change mode, DEL takes
a digit back.
tools.summary: Five chemistry calculations, each opening on a worked example with the substitution written out.
tools.body: Moles from a mass, concentration, the gas equation, dilution, and yield or atom economy. Every mode starts with numbers in place so the shape of the answer is visible before you type, and the panel shows the substitution the calculator did, not just the number.
points: 4 g of NaOH, Mr 40: n = 4 / 40 = 0.1 mol, 6.02e22 particles.
0.1 mol in 0.25 dm3 is 0.4 mol/dm3; the panel restates it in cm3.
100 kPa, 24 dm3 and 298 K give 0.9686 mol from n = pV / RT.
Diluting 20 cm3 of 0.5 into 250 cm3 gives 0.04 mol/dm3.

tools.help:
Lab graph
Type a measured pair and its error,
press EXE, and repeat. F2 draws
the graph with a bar up and down
through every point and the line of
best fit.

The gradient comes with its standard
error, from the residuals, and r
squared says how well the line
fits. Fewer than three points leave
nothing to measure the error against,
so it is left off.

The axes hold the whole bar, not
just the centre, so a measurement
never runs off the top.

Up to twelve points. F1 clears,
F3 puts the example back, DEL on an
empty field drops the last point.

Keys: digits type, LEFT/RIGHT pick
a field, EXE adds the point.
tools.summary: Plot measured points with their uncertainties and read the gradient, its standard error and r squared.
tools.body: A lab graph is a scatter with bars, a line of best fit and the two numbers for the conclusion. Type x, y and the error for each point, then F2 draws the whole thing: the axes hold the full bar, so a measurement can never run off the top.
points: The gradient comes with its standard error, from the residuals, not a guess.
Fewer than three points leave nothing to check the fit against, so no error is quoted.
Rounded axes: the range is a whole number of 1, 2, 2.5 or 5 steps.
Up to twelve points, and the fit updates as each one is added.
